evidence.outcome: impact of manual corrections on contour accuracy
evidence.effect: corrections significantly improved left CTVn1 across all metrics, but overall only a small number of cases had significantly different contours after correction (right CTVp DSC improved by 0.02 +/- 0.05)
evidence.quote: These results indicate that, although corrections were made in most of the cases, only for a small number of cases these corrections were actually significantly different.

evidence.title: Incorporation of CAD (computer-aided detection) with thin-slice lung CT in routine 18F-FDG PET/CT imaging read-out protocol for detection of lung nodules
evidence.outcome: clinician filtering of CAD false-positive nodule detections
evidence.effect: Readers accepted an average of 282 CAD nodules and rejected 1685 false markings (16.8 false positives per scan)
evidence.quote: In the given 100 patients, CADp showed total of 1967 nodules, of which on average 282 were accepted by the three readers, and remaining average 1685 were rejected as false markings.

evidence.title: Real-world validation of Artificial Intelligence-based Computed Tomography auto-contouring for prostate cancer radiotherapy planning
evidence.venue: Physics and imaging in radiation oncology
evidence.outcome: edited contour agreement
evidence.effect: After editing, DSC improved p ≤ 0.002; seminal vesicles 0.76 vs 0.65 and prostate 0.86 vs 0.82.
evidence.quote: After editing, DSC significantly improved (p ≤ 0.002) for both OARs and CTVs: the larger gain was found for seminal vesicles (0.76 vs 0.65) and for prostate (0.86 vs 0.82).

evidence.title: OSAIRIS: Lessons Learned From the Hospital-Based Implementation and Evaluation of an Open-Source Deep-Learning Model for Radiotherapy Image Segmentation
evidence.venue: Clinical oncology (Royal College of Radiologists (Great Britain))
evidence.outcome: clinician correction of AI errors
evidence.effect: Clinicians removed 72% of head and neck errors and 81% of prostate errors in editing.
evidence.quote: Most errors, however, were corrected by clinicians, with 72% of the head and neck errors 81% of the prostate errors removed in the editing step.

evidence.title: Artificial intelligence-assisted delineation for postoperative radiotherapy in patients with lung cancer: a prospective, multi-center, cohort study
evidence.outcome: Clinician-edited AI contour accuracy
evidence.quote: AI-assisted delineation achieved significantly higher accuracy compared to unmodified AI auto-contouring and fully manual delineation by radiation oncologists, with median HD, MDA, and DCS values of 20.03 vs. 21.55 mm, 2.57 vs. 3.06 mm, 0.745 vs. 0.703 (all P<0.05) for CTV, respectively.

evidence.title: A randomized controlled trial on evaluating clinician-supervised generative AI for decision support
evidence.outcome: Decision accuracy in simulated CPR with clinician-supervised vs autonomous ChatGPT vs paper guide
evidence.effect: Supervised-ChatGPT group showed significantly higher decision accuracy than paper guide and ChatGPT groups, though scenario completion time was longer. In one instance ChatGPT suggested a risky option.
evidence.quote: Results indicate that the Supervised-ChatGPT group showed significantly higher decision accuracy compared to the paper guide and ChatGPT groups, although the scenario completion time was longer.

evidence.title: Safety of human-AI cooperative decision-making within intensive care: A physical simulation study
evidence.outcome: Physician rejection of unsafe versus safe AI treatment recommendations
evidence.effect: Unsafe AI recommendations were stopped more often than safe ones (83 ± 4%, 95% CI: 0.75–0.91 vs 29 ± 4%, 95% CI: 0.21–0.37, p < 0.0001), rising to 92 ± 3% with senior consultation.
evidence.quote: In total, unsafe AI recommendations were stopped more often than safe AI recommendations (83 ± 4%, 95% CI: 0.75–0.91 vs. 29 ± 4%, 95% CI: 0.21–0.37, p < 0.0001).

evidence.title: Integrating AI into clinical education: evaluating general practice trainees' proficiency in distinguishing AI-generated hallucinations and impacting factors
evidence.outcome: Trainees' accuracy and sensitivity in detecting ChatGPT-4o hallucinations in simulated clinical questions
evidence.effect: Mean accuracy of detecting the 87 hallucinations was 55.0%, mean sensitivity (d') 0.39, showing trainees often failed to verify and catch incorrect AI outputs.
evidence.quote: The mean accuracy of detecting these hallucinations was 55.0%, and the mean sensitivity (d') was 0.39.

evidence.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence Models in Clinical Infectious Disease Consultations: A Cross-Sectional Analysis Among Specialists and Resident Trainees
evidence.outcome: Whether clinician reviewers detect harmful or inaccurate AI outputs
evidence.effect: Specialists were five times more likely than residents to rate responses harmless; post hoc analysis showed specialists may disregard conflicting or inaccurate information. Fewer than two-fifths of responses were deemed harmless.
evidence.quote: Post hoc analysis revealed that specialists may inadvertently disregard conflicting or inaccurate information in their assessments.

evidence.title: Comparison of Artificial Intelligence Models and Human Experts in Managing Dyslipidemia: Assessment of Adherence to Clinical Guidelines
evidence.outcome: simulated LDL-C target attainment
evidence.effect: AI draft recommendations with professor supervision achieved 92%, exceeding any single respondent group.
evidence.quote: Of particular clinical significance, a combined workflow incorporating AI-generated draft recommendations with professor supervision yielded a simulated target attainment rate of 92%, exceeding the performance of any single respondent group and approaching the ideal clinical target of >90% guideline adherence.

evidence.title: Large language model as clinical decision support system augments medication safety in 16 clinical specialties
evidence.outcome: Serious-error detection
evidence.effect: LLM alone caught 52% of serious errors; co-pilot mode caught 66%.
evidence.quote: LLMs alone were capable of catching 52% of serious errors, while that improved with co-pilot mode to 66%.
evidence.sample_unit: simulated prescribing error scenarios (40 vignettes) reviewed by 6 pharmacists

evidence.title: Human-in-the-Loop Performance of LLM-Assisted Arterial Blood Gas Interpretation: A Single-Center Retrospective Study
evidence.outcome: Agreement with expert reference on primary and secondary acid-base disorders, LLM-S (user interpretation) vs LLM-I (LLM interpretation)
evidence.effect: APSD kappa rose from 0.61-0.65 with LLM interpretation (LLM-I) to 0.81-0.91 with user-supervised interpretation (LLM-S); AMA kappa from 0.48-0.76 to ≥0.85.
evidence.quote: In the LLM-S method, APSD agreement improved substantially, with κ = 0.91 for ChatGPT and κ = 0.81 for both Copilot and Gemini.

evidence.title: Evaluating human-in-the-loop strategies for artificial intelligence-enabled translation of patient discharge instructions: a multidisciplinary analysis
evidence.outcome: Translation quality ratings of ChatGPT-4o alone vs professional linguist post-edited (human-in-the-loop) output
evidence.effect: Human-in-the-loop translations were comparable or better than professional translations in all languages (Armenian overall quality 3.9 vs 3.6, p=0.01), whereas ChatGPT-4o alone was poorest for Armenian (2.4) and Somali.
evidence.quote: For example, the mean overall domain rating for Armenian human-in-the-loop translations was 3.9 (3.7–4.2) for human-in-the-loop and 3.6 (3.4–3.9) for professional translations, a difference of 0.3 (0.1–0.5) ( p = 0.01).
evidence.sample_unit: evaluators (12 linguists, 16 clinicians, 14 family caregivers) rating 20 discharge instruction texts translated into 6 languages

evidence.title: The impact of artificial intelligence-driven decision support on uncertain antimicrobial prescribing: a randomised, multimethod study
evidence.outcome: incorrect advice review
evidence.effect: Clinicians were able to identify and ignore incorrect advice; no numeric estimate reported.
evidence.quote: Case vignette completion times and many decisions were equivalent between SOC and CDSS interventions, with clinicians able to identify and ignore incorrect advice.

evidence.title: Digital Pathology with AI for Cervical Biopsies: Diagnostic Accuracy at the CIN2+ Threshold
evidence.outcome: clinician correction of high-consequence AI errors
evidence.effect: Clinician review of AI outputs restored ACIS from 13/20 to 18/20 and reduced false-positive squamous cell carcinoma calls from 4 to 1.
evidence.quote: After expert adjudication in the EE + P2 condition, ACIS was restored to 18/20 and SCC was reduced to 1/20, demonstrating that the human reviewer corrected virtually all high-consequence AI errors.

evidence.title: Diagnosing growth in low-grade gliomas with and without artificial intelligence-measured longitudinal volume measurements: A retrospective observational study
evidence.outcome: False positive and false negative rates of AI volumetry with versus without physician review
evidence.effect: AI without human review had 25% false positives (4/16) and 8.33% false negatives (4/48); with physician review all 7 negative controls were correctly identified as stable.
evidence.quote: The performance of the volumetric analysis using the change-point method varied significantly depending on whether human review was involved.

evidence.title: Digitally Assisted Clinical Decision-Making in Traditional Chinese Medicine: Comparative Study of 5 Large Language Models
evidence.outcome: Physician adoption, modification, and rejection of AI-generated plans after review
evidence.effect: Of 400 decisions, 74.25% adopted, 24% modified, 1.75% rejected; medication recommendations had 32% adoption and 62% modification.
evidence.quote: Collaboration pattern analysis across 400 total decisions revealed high acceptance rates—74.25% (297/400) adoption, 24% (96/400) modification, and 1.75% (7/400) rejection.
evidence.sample_unit: TCM practitioners (plus 160 exam questions, 30 cases, 5 clinical cases for human-AI comparison)

evidence.title: Strategic Governance of Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Clinical Algorithm Development: Formative Evaluation of the Semiautomatic Clinical Algorithm Development Framework
evidence.outcome: Whether human expert verification of AI outputs caught errors versus a fully autonomous AI workflow
evidence.effect: S-ACAD with 19 human interventions: no critical safety errors found by 2 external specialists; F-ACAD without human review produced 17 issues (9 high-priority). Expert changed AI-generated diazepam pathway to require calling 911. Single case.
evidence.quote: Although F-ACAD reviewed more sources and produced a more complex algorithm, its own AI critics identified 17 issues requiring correction, including 9 high-priority concerns related to US standard-of-care compliance, emergency-response clarity, and parent-friendly communication.
evidence.sample_unit: algorithm development executions (single expert, single clinical topic: pediatric febrile seizures)

evidence.title: Harnessing Large Language Models in Neonatal Intraventricular Hemorrhage: Exploring Retrieval Augmented Generation Methodology for Prognostic Variable Discovery
evidence.outcome: Whether manual validation of LLM outputs catches hallucinated or incomplete content
evidence.effect: Manual validation excluded hallucinated references from 39 LLM-identified studies (28 retained); authors conclude LLM outputs were susceptible to hallucinations and incomplete synthesis, requiring human validation.
evidence.quote: However, LLM outputs were susceptible to hallucinations and incomplete data synthesis, underscoring the need for rigorous clinical oversight and human validation to ensure reliability.

evidence.title: Using ChatGPT‑4.0 to Address Nurse Scheduling Challenges in a Cardiology Clinic
evidence.outcome: Whether human review corrected gaps in ChatGPT-generated nurse schedules
evidence.effect: Hybrid 4×10/5×8 schedule met daily coverage and maintained equity but gave no redundancy for absences; human review resolved role-specific gaps.
evidence.quote: A hybrid 4×10/5×8 model met daily coverage 5 Outpatient Care Center (OCC), 1 Heart Center (HC), and maintained equity, but provided no redundancy for absences; human review resolved role‑specific gaps.

evidence.title: A prospective multicenter trial of deep learning auto-segmentation for organs at risk in thoracic radiotherapy
evidence.outcome: Contour accuracy after physician review and modification versus unmodified AI outputs
evidence.effect: Physician revision significantly improved accuracy for 6 out of 11 OARs (54.5%); mean vDSC increased from 0.896 to 0.902, and mean HD95 decreased from 5.62 mm to 5.20 mm.
evidence.quote: AI-assisted delineation also achieved significantly higher accuracy than AI delineation for 6 out of 11 OARs (54.5%): the heart, aorta, liver, trachea, spinal cord, and esophagus (Fig. 2a, b and Supplementary Fig. 3 ).

evidence.title: Fact-Checking Large Language Model Responses to a Health Care Prompt: Comparative Study
evidence.outcome: Whether LLM fact-checking of its own response catches errors versus expert verification
evidence.effect: GPT-4o and OpenBioLLM-70B had 86% agreement with experts on the acne scenario. Both LLM fact-checks missed the understated urgency of stopping isotretinoin and the folic acid issue. Experts identified 3 mostly-true claims that the LLMs called true.
evidence.quote: The experts disagreed with the LLM classification of the claim about the use of folic acid because the response understated the importance of taking folic acid during pregnancy.
evidence.sample_unit: clinical claims (plus one acne scenario with 16 expert-identified claims)

evidence.title: Human-in-the-Loop Enhances Machine Learning Inference in Intraoperative Optical Coherence Tomography Glioma Imaging
evidence.outcome: Clinician verification of AI segmentation outputs catching AI errors
evidence.effect: Surgeons overrode algorithmic false positives in 69% (9/13) of cases; HITL accuracy 94% vs SVM 84%.
evidence.quote: They successfully override algorithmic noise in 69% (9 out of 13) of false-positive cases because tissue topology and signal margins provide vital contextual cues that the algorithm currently lacks.
evidence.sample_unit: intraoperative OCT scans (27 patients; 5 neurosurgeon raters)

evidence.title: Performance of the Techcyte AI-based image analysis system for coproparasitological diagnosis in clinical stool specimens: a retrospective evaluation study
evidence.outcome: Whether operator verification of AI detections corrects AI errors (artifacts)
evidence.effect: Artifacts in 162/178 (91.01%) specimens on raw analysis; operator review dismissed them, raising PPA/NPA to 96.62%/93.33%.
evidence.quote: Operator review was essential for accurate interpretation, to avoid diagnostic issues, and mainly to discard artifact detections.

evidence.title: Securing Safety and Quality in AI-generated Patient Education: A Nurse-led Methodological Framework Integrating Kolcaba's Comfort Theory
evidence.outcome: Clinical accuracy/hallucination mitigation and content validity of AI patient education after nurse clinical refinement
evidence.effect: Protocol mitigated AI hallucinations; expert panel (n=3) consensus Content Validity Index 0.93-0.95 indicated clinical safety.
evidence.quote: High expert consensus (CVI: 0.93-0.95) demonstrated clinical safety, proving nursing expertise is a mandatory safety layer.
evidence.sample_unit: expert panel reviewers (evaluating AI-generated education materials for 3 disease cases)

evidence.title: Radiologist Detection of Deficiencies in LLM-Generated Patient Communications About Radiology Reports: A Multi-Reader Study
evidence.venue: Journal of imaging informatics in medicine
evidence.outcome: Radiologist sensitivity for detecting deficient LLM answers to patient questions about radiology reports
evidence.effect: Individual sensitivity 81.4% to 96.5%; readers missed 5.6-11.1% of clinically significant errors; single reader missed avg 12.4% of deficiencies.
evidence.quote: For clinically significant errors, readers missed 5.6-11.1% of cases.
evidence.sample_unit: LLM-generated answers to simulated patient questions

evidence.title: Real-world evaluation of medication recommendation workflows: Retrieval augmentation, physician-RAG collaborative workflow, and prescribing quality
evidence.outcome: Prescribing completeness, precision, and Jaccard index under physician collaboration
evidence.effect: Physician-RAG collaborative showed CORE recall 1.000 (95 % CI, 0.999-1.000), ALT recall 0.955 (95 % CI, 0.945-0.964), overall recall 0.978, precision 0.963, and Jaccard index 0.943
evidence.quote: Physician-RAG collaborative showed the highest CORE recall (1.000; 95 % CI, 0.999-1.000), ALT recall (0.955; 95 % CI, 0.945-0.964), overall recall (0.978; 95 % CI, 0.973-0.982), precision (0.963; 95 % CI, 0.957-0.969), and Jaccard index (0.943; 95 % CI, 0.935-0.949).

evidence.title: End-to-End Pipeline Integrating Local Small Language Models and Machine Learning for Data Extraction and Stroke Outcome Prediction in Emergency Department
evidence.outcome: Extraction accuracy and F1 score after clinician human-in-the-loop review
evidence.effect: Accuracy increased from 86.0% to 97.0% (95% CI, 95.7% to 98.3%) and F1 from 0.813 to 0.920 (95% CI, 0.879 to 0.961)
evidence.quote: The final HITL review achieved the highest data fidelity, yielding an accuracy of 97.0% (95% CI, 95.7% to 98.3%), F1 score of 0.920 (95% CI, 0.879 to 0.961), and variable-level F1 of 0.902 (95% CI, 0.841 to 0.962), with grounding accuracy increasing to 93.2% (95% CI, 91.7% to 94.7%).

evidence.title: Enhancing the Morphological Detection of Cytomegalovirus in Gastrointestinal Biopsies: A Deep Learning Approach Trained on IHC-Validated Ground Truth
evidence.outcome: Whether pathologist verification of AI-labeled candidates filters out CMV mimics
evidence.effect: Reported qualitatively: the human-in-the-loop workflow mitigated mimics such as reactive endothelial nuclei; no numeric error-catch rate given.
evidence.quote: The "human-in-the-loop" workflow successfully mitigated common mimics, such as reactive endothelial nuclei, through automated candidate labeling and rapid pathologist verification.

evidence.title: Artificial Intelligence-Enabled ECGs for Atrial Fibrillation Identification and Enhanced Oral Anticoagulant Adoption: A Pragmatic Randomized Clinical Trial
evidence.venue: Journal of the American Heart Association
evidence.outcome: Inappropriate NOAC prescriptions following false-positive AI-ECG AF alerts
evidence.effect: 48 (intervention) and 35 (control) potential AI errors; only 1 intervention patient received NOAC, clinically justified by later AF; no off-label NOAC prescriptions attributable to AI errors.
evidence.quote: As such, there were no instances of off‐label NOAC prescription attributable to potential AI‐ECG errors.

evidence.title: Design and Architecture of a Generative-AI-Supported, Nonphysician-Delivered Model for GDMT Optimization in HFrEF: The ASSIST-HF Trial
evidence.outcome: Safety disagreements between AI GDMT recommendations and supervising cardiologist
evidence.effect: No safety disagreements between VA and clinician recommendations were reported across the 12-week VA arm (30 patients).
evidence.quote: Patient-reported acceptability, appropriateness and feasibility scores were high, with no safety disagreements between VA and clinician recommendations.

evidence.title: Using a Machine-Learning Algorithm to Identify Palliative Care Needs in a Primary Care Population: A Pilot Study
evidence.outcome: Positive predictive value against specialist assessment of consultation appropriateness
evidence.effect: PPV was 0.18; specialists accepted 273/1512 presented cases. Nonacceptance could reflect already-addressed needs or unsuitable referral timing, rather than absence of palliative care needs.
evidence.quote: In this trial, the algorithm had a PPV of 0.18, with the palliative care specialist accepting 273/1512 cases presented across both arms.

evidence.title: Implementation and clinical evaluation of an in-house thoracic auto-segmentation model for 0.35 T magnetic resonance imaging guided radiotherapy
evidence.venue: Physics and imaging in radiation oncology
evidence.outcome: Incomplete auto-generated organ contours identified during clinical correction
evidence.effect: Aorta and heart auto-segmentations contained missing slices in 5 cases, with one to three missing slices each.
evidence.quote: These anomalies were primarily due to missing slices in the auto-segmentations for these structures, which were present in 5 cases with one to three missing slices each and disproportionately impacted totalAPL.

evidence.title: Assessing the User Experience of an LLM-Based Conversational Assistant in Diabetes Mellitus Care
evidence.outcome: Hallucinations and appropriateness of LLM health suggestions for patients with clinical constraints
evidence.effect: No factual hallucinations were generated, but some accurate general health suggestions could be inappropriate for users with specific clinical constraints.
evidence.quote: While MarIA did not generate factual hallucinations, some general health suggestions-though accurate in isolation-could be inappropriate for users with specific clinical constraints.

evidence.title: ChatGPT-4o as a decision-support tool in a urological tumour board: a prospective evaluation
evidence.venue: Clinical & translational oncology : official publication of the Federation of Spanish Oncology Societies and of the National Cancer Institute of Mexico
evidence.outcome: Model errors documented in AI outputs, including among highly concordant outputs
evidence.effect: Model errors in 19/106 discussions (17.9%), including 13/84 (15.5%) rated highly concordant and 6/22 (27.3%) rated below threshold; four errors (3.8%) potentially harmful
evidence.quote: The post hoc review documented model errors in 19/106 discussions (17.9%), including 13/84 (15.5%) discussions rated highly concordant and 6/22 (27.3%) rated below that threshold; four errors (3.8%) were graded as potentially harmful.

evidence.title: Augmenting Head and Neck Multidisciplinary Tumor Board Recommendations With Locally Run Large Language Models: Prospective Evaluation of Real-World Implementation
evidence.outcome: Rate of potentially hazardous information in LLM outputs rated by MDT members
evidence.effect: Potentially hazardous information in 27% (25/93) of ratings for gemma-3-12b and 17% (14/83) of ratings for gpt-oss-20b.
evidence.quote: MDT members stated potentially hazardous information in 27% (25/93, 95% CI 18%-37%) of ratings for gemma-3-12b and 17% (14/83, 95% CI 9%-26%) of ratings for gpt-oss-20b.

evidence.title: Artificial Intelligence-enhanced cardiac MRI reporting: expert validation and patient-centered outcomes
evidence.venue: The international journal of cardiovascular imaging
evidence.outcome: Rate of high-risk AI-generated clinical recommendations rated by expert cardiologists
evidence.effect: High-risk recommendations affected 1 patient (1.3%) for patient-directed and 5 patients (6.7%) for physician-directed content; correctness 3.73 and 3.52; mean harm 2.10 and 2.16.
evidence.quote: High-risk recommendations were infrequent but not negligible, affecting 1 patient (1.3%) for patient-directed and 5 patients (6.7%) for physician-directed content, and were concentrated in clinically complex cases.

evidence.title: From Output Errors to Workflow Harm: A Practitioner-Audit Method for LLM-Mediated Research
evidence.outcome: Frequency of verification failures among LLM incidents recorded in research and informatics workflows
evidence.effect: Verification failure was one of four tied most frequent categories (n=7 of 45 incidents); the claimed-verification gap was described as a measurable failure mode distinct from hallucination.
evidence.quote: Four categories tied as most frequent: verification failure, factual numerical error, tool-behavior misunderstanding, and citation or reference formatting (n=7 each).

evidence.title: Cardiac anatomic digital twins: findings from a single national centre
evidence.outcome: Need for manual correction of AI-generated anatomic twin segmentations
evidence.effect: Manual corrections of the AI-generated digital anatomic twins were always necessary; the AI only facilitated rapid creation.
evidence.quote: While artificial intelligence facilitated the rapid creation of digital anatomic twins, manual corrections were always necessary.

evidence.title: Integrating large language models in biostatistical workflows for clinical and translational research
evidence.venue: Journal of clinical and translational science
evidence.outcome: Self-reported significant errors in LLM outputs used by biostatisticians, including hallucinated functions
evidence.effect: 29 of 41 respondents (70.7%) reported significant errors, including incorrect code, statistical misinterpretations, and hallucinated functions; verification strategies included expertise, external validation, debugging, and manual inspection.
evidence.quote: however, 29 of 41 respondents (70.7%) reported significant errors, including incorrect code, statistical misinterpretations, and hallucinated functions.

evidence.title: Safety of a large language model-based clinical decision support system in African primary healthcare
evidence.outcome: Actively harmful LLM recommendations and whether they persisted in final documentation
evidence.effect: Actively harmful recommendations in 115 encounters (7.8%, 95% CI 6.5-9.3), with 67 appearing in the final documentation; clinicians did not modify documentation in 917 encounters (62%).
evidence.quote: Safety assessments identified actively harmful recommendations from the large language model in 115 encounters (7.8%, 95% CI 6.5-9.3), with 67 such recommendations appearing in the final documentation.

evidence.title: Artificial Intelligence-Generated Electronic Medical Record Summarization in Breast Surgical Oncology
evidence.outcome: Frequency and criticality of errors in AI summaries that clinicians would need to verify
evidence.effect: Errors were noted in 25 (40%) surveys, with 13 (52%) classified as critical (treatment-impacting).
evidence.quote: Errors were noted in 25 (40%) surveys, with 13 (52%) classified as critical (treatment-impacting).

evidence.title: Informal use of generative artificial intelligence by nursing interns during clinical placement: A multi-stakeholder interpretive description
evidence.outcome: Whether staff verify AI outputs before acting on them
evidence.effect: Verification was universally endorsed by stakeholders but unevenly enacted in practice (qualitative theme; no numbers reported).
evidence.quote: Five interconnected themes emerged: (1) multilevel discretionary rule-making in a policy vacuum; (2) a universally endorsed but unevenly enacted verification imperative; (3) intuitive risk stratification; (4) tensions between standardised AI outputs and embodied nursing care; and (5) a cross-stakeholder call for institutional frameworks.
evidence.sample_unit: interview participants (nursing interns, preceptors, head nurses, administrators, IT specialists, quality officer)

evidence.title: Agentic clinical reasoning over longitudinal myeloma records: a retrospective evaluation against expert consensus
evidence.outcome: Rate and clinical severity of system errors versus expert disagreement
evidence.effect: System error rate 12.2% vs expert disagreement 13.6%; 57.8% of system errors clinically significant vs 18.8% of expert disagreements.
evidence.quote: The system error rate (12.2%) was comparable to expert disagreement (13.6%), but severity was inverted: 57.8% of system errors were clinically significant versus 18.8% of expert disagreements.

evidence.title: Completeness and Quality of Neurology Referral Letters Generated by a Large Language Model for Standardized Scenarios
evidence.outcome: Content gaps and management variability in LLM-generated neurology referral letters
evidence.effect: Noticeable gaps in history of present illness and physical findings in 72% (36/50) of letters; case management score varied (mean 2.18, SD 0.85).
evidence.quote: Noticeable gaps in content, particularly in history of present illness and physical findings, were identified in 72% (36/50) of the letters.

evidence.title: Automation Bias in Large Language Model Assisted Diagnostic Reasoning Among AI-Trained Physicians
evidence.outcome: Physicians' failure to verify erroneous LLM outputs, degrading diagnostic reasoning
evidence.effect: Flawed LLM recommendations reduced diagnostic reasoning accuracy from 84.9% to 73.3% and top-choice accuracy from 90.5% to 76.1%.
evidence.quote: Voluntary deference to flawed AI output highlights critical patient safety risk, necessitating robust safeguards to ensure human oversight before widespread clinical deployment.

evidence.title: The Art of AI Dialogue: Evaluating Applied AI Literacy in Medical Students Using a Performance-Based Rubric — A Single-Institution Observational Study
evidence.outcome: Extent to which students verified AI-generated content and recognized bias
evidence.effect: Verification & Critical Thinking (bias recognition) scored M = 0.41 (SD = 0.71) of 3, the lowest of four domains (Friedman χ²(3) = 50.36, p < 0.001).
evidence.quote: Domain-level analysis revealed the highest performance in Transparency (M = 2.08, SD = 0.55) and Integration (M = 1.64, SD = 0.67), while Purposefulness (M = 1.33, SD = 0.69) and Verification & Critical Thinking (M = 0.41, SD = 0.71) were significantly lower.
evidence.sample_unit: third-year medical students (research proposals with AI chat transcripts)

evidence.title: Systematic Evaluation of Multilingual Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Gastrointestinal Tumor Board Decision Support
evidence.outcome: Clinical appropriateness of residual discordant LLM recommendations in optimal configurations
evidence.effect: Approximately 60% of residual discordant cases represented clinically inappropriate recommendations rather than acceptable alternatives.
evidence.quote: Among residual discordant cases in optimal configurations, approximately 60% represented clinically inappropriate recommendations rather than acceptable therapeutic alternatives.

evidence.title: Errors, Hallucinations, and Clinical Impact of General-Purpose Multimodal Large Language Models in Histopathology
evidence.outcome: Prevalence of errors and hallucinations, including in correct diagnoses, that clinician verification would need to catch
evidence.effect: 79.9% of strictly correct diagnoses also contained at least one error or hallucination; every strictly incorrect diagnosis contained an error and/or hallucination.
evidence.quote: Every strictly incorrect diagnosis contained an error and/or hallucination, while 79.9% of strictly correct diagnoses also contained at least one.
evidence.sample_unit: LLM outputs (153 pathology cases x 4 LLMs)

evidence.title: Evaluating Large Language Models for Drafting Emergency Department Discharge Summaries
evidence.outcome: Prevalence of hallucination and omission errors in LLM-generated ED discharge summaries
evidence.effect: GPT-4: 33% error-free; inaccuracies in 10%, hallucinations in 42%, omissions of clinically relevant information in 47%. GPT-3.5-turbo: 10% error-free.
evidence.quote: Summaries generated by GPT-4 were mostly accurate, with inaccuracies found in only 10% of cases, however, 42% of the summaries exhibited hallucinations and 47% omitted clinically relevant information.

evidence.title: Integrating AI in Clinical Education: Evaluating General Practice Residents’ Proficiency in Distinguishing AI-Generated Hallucinations and Its Impacting Factors
evidence.outcome: Residents' accuracy and sensitivity in detecting AI-generated hallucinations in ChatGPT answers
evidence.effect: Mean accuracy 55% ± 4.3%; mean d' 0.39 ± 0.33; residents struggled to identify AI errors, particularly in clinical cases.
evidence.quote: The mean (SD) accuracy was 55% ±4.3%, and the mean (SD) sensitivity (d') was 0.39 ± 0.33.

evidence.title: Assessing the Limitations of Large Language Models in Clinical Practice Guideline-concordant Treatment Decision-making on Real-world Data
evidence.outcome: hallucinations in treatment outputs
evidence.effect: Instances of hallucinations occurred in all LLMs tested.
evidence.quote: Qualitative analysis revealed instances of hallucinations in all LLMs tested.

evidence.title: Clinical evaluation of a deep learning segmentation model including manual adjustments afterwards for locally advanced breast cancer
evidence.venue: Technical innovations & patient support in radiation oncology
evidence.outcome: clinically unusable AI contours
evidence.effect: CTVp, CTVn1, and CTVn4 were not usable in 7, 6, and 4 cases, respectively.
evidence.quote: The CTVp was found not to be usable in a total of seven cases, CTVn1 in six cases and CTVn4 in four cases.

evidence.title: Could artificial intelligence write mental health nursing care plans?
evidence.venue: Journal of psychiatric and mental health nursing
evidence.outcome: Errors in ChatGPT-generated mental health care plan for self-harm case, evaluated by clinical authors
evidence.effect: Care plan incorporated some DBT principles but had significant errors and limitations, with a reasonable likelihood of harm if used without expert correction; errors may go unnoticed because output looks superficially reasonable.
evidence.quote: Given ChatGPT's ability to provide superficially reasonable outputs there is a risk that errors may go unnoticed and thus increase the likelihood of patient harms.
evidence.sample_unit: ChatGPT-generated care plans for one fictitious patient

evidence.title: Incorporation of CAD (computer-aided detection) with thin-slice lung CT in routine 18F-FDG PET/CT imaging read-out protocol for detection of lung nodules
evidence.outcome: false-positive CAD markings
evidence.effect: CADp showed 1967 nodules; on average 282 were accepted and 1685 rejected as false markings.
evidence.quote: In the given 100 patients, CADp showed total of 1967 nodules, of which on average 282 were accepted by the three readers, and remaining average 1685 were rejected as false markings.

evidence.title: Can Chatbot Artificial Intelligence Replace Infectious Diseases Physicians in the Management of Bloodstream Infections? A Prospective Cohort Study
evidence.venue: Clinical infectious diseases : an official publication of the Infectious Diseases Society of America
evidence.outcome: Clinical harm potential of unverified chatbot recommendations
evidence.effect: Harmful management plans in 7 (16%) cases; authors conclude use without consultant input is hazardous.
evidence.quote: The use of ChatGPT-4 without consultant input remains hazardous when seeking expert medical advice in 2023, especially for severe IDs.
evidence.sample_unit: patients (consecutive ID consultations for first positive blood culture)

evidence.title: Clinical decision-making in benzodiazepine deprescribing by healthcare providers vs. AI-assisted approach
evidence.outcome: Accuracy and ambiguity of ChatGPT-4 deprescribing outputs versus HCP judgement

evidence.title: Evaluating ChatGPT as a patient resource for frequently asked questions about lung cancer surgery-a pilot study

evidence.title: Generative artificial intelligence writing open notes: A mixed methods assessment of the functionality of GPT 3.5 and GPT 4.0

evidence.title: Comparing physician and large language model responses to influenza patient questions in the online health community

evidence.title: Safety of human-AI cooperative decision-making within intensive care: A physical simulation study

evidence.title: Human-AI collaboration in large language model-assisted brain MRI differential diagnosis: a usability study

evidence.title: AI-assisted decision-making in mild traumatic brain injury

evidence.title: Summarizing clinical evidence utilizing large language models for cancer treatments: a blinded comparative analysis

commentary.bottom_line: Studies comparing AI output alone with AI output after clinician review, mostly in imaging, radiotherapy contouring, and screening, report fewer false positives and better agreement after review, but most measure surrogate outcomes and none tests a verification requirement as a policy. In a real-deployment study of generative AI in Kenya, clinicians did not modify 62% of AI-drafted documentation and 67 harmful recommendations reached the final record, which suggests that requiring verification may not ensure it occurs.

perspectives.view: Of 25 listed tests, one is an RCT, and it reports that clinicians disagreed with 20.7% of electronic AKI diagnoses rather than reporting patient outcomes. Most other studies are descriptive or replay designs that measure PPV or contour overlap. Results agree for imaging and contouring but diverge for generative AI and teledermatology, and indirectness lowers certainty to low.

Specialist overread raised PPV from 47.7% to 95.5% with sensitivity unchanged, and radiologists reported only one of 381 AI false positives. Review can also remove true findings, as teledermatology review lowered sensitivity from 82.5% to 75.3%. In Kenya, 67 harmful LLM recommendations reached final documentation, and residents detected hallucinations with 55% accuracy.

Verification fidelity varied in real workflows, as clinicians did not modify LLM-drafted documentation in 62% of encounters, and interviewed staff endorsed verification but enacted it unevenly. A simulated co-pilot mode reported better detection of drug-related problems than an autonomous LLM, which suggests that the design of the review step may matter as much as the rule requiring it.

Readers rejected 16.8 false CAD markings per scan, expert chart review removed 208 of 388 model-flagged patients from outreach, and pathologists reviewed 1733 alerted benign cases, of which 128 changed, so review adds workload. Editing AI contours took 12.3 minutes versus 25.0 minutes for manual contouring, which suggests review may still save time compared with working without AI.

One deployment in Puerto Rico served a racial and ethnic minority population, and pathologist review resolved all 17 false-positive validation alerts. The Kenyan study, set in a lower-resource health system, found that verification often did not happen. No test reported enrolling Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients.

One case report describes a team that judged an AI pneumothorax alert inconsistent with the clinical picture, excluded it by CT, and avoided an unneeded procedure. In a simulation, most of 38 intensivists rejected unsafe AI advice and many sought senior help. A hazard report notes that erroneous AI care plans can look reasonable, so cursory review may leave patients exposed.

commentary.research_gap: No study compares units with and without a formal verification requirement, and few measure patient outcomes such as treatment errors or harm. Studies of generative AI workflows could measure how often clinicians catch seeded errors, the time review adds, and whether review design, such as source links, checklists, or attestation prompts, changes detection rates.
commentary.underserved_note: No test of the practice reported including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. One test took place in Puerto Rico with a racial and ethnic minority focus, and one took place in Kenya, where verification frequently failed. Health systems serving these populations therefore cannot assume that verification performs as reported in the imaging and contouring studies.
